title: Set the goalposts first
principle: Test small first, and decide beforehand what result means yes.

screens.text: Let me tell you a story about idli batter. In 2006, PC Musthafa and his cousins started iD in Bengaluru with ₹50,000 and one small room. They put 100 packets into 20 stores, and before going further, they gave themselves a target and a deadline: six months.

screens.prompt: Of those first 100 packets, how many do you think came back unsold?
screens.why: About 90. Musthafa said 90 of every 100 packets used to come back, so they sold fewer than 10 a day. They were nowhere near their target, and six months came and went.

screens.prompt: Six months passed and they'd missed their target. What do you think they did next?

options.label: Kept the target and fixed the batter
Lowered the target and called it a success
Rented a big factory to look serious

screens.why: Exactly. They didn't move the target or pretend they'd made the date. They kept working until they reached it, three months late, and Musthafa says getting the batter right took about nine months. Later, iD was in 1,000 stores across Bengaluru.

wrong.b: I see the thinking: lower the bar, and you've passed. But a target you move after the test can't tell you anything. They kept theirs and reached it three months late.
wrong.c: That's betting big before the idea has passed its test. With 90 of every 100 packets coming back, a factory would only make more packets to come back. They stayed small and fixed the batter first.

screens.title: Set the goalposts first
screens.text: Think of football. If you move the goalposts after the kick, any shot can be a goal, and the score means nothing. iD set its target before it knew how sales would go. That's called pre-set success criteria: the yes number and the check date, written down first.

screens.prompt: Musthafa counted packets sold, not packets sent to stores. Why does that matter so much?

options.label: Packets sent are easier to count
Anyone can send packets; only buyers decide sales

screens.why: Exactly. You can push 100 packets into stores any day you like, but you can't make shoppers buy them. Pick a yes number that's hard to fake, and the test can't flatter you.

wrong.a: They are easier to count, but they're also easy to fake. You could push 100 packets out tomorrow and 'pass'. Sales are decided by buyers, so they tell the truth.
wrong.b: Stores don't mind either way. The point is for you: packets sent go up whenever you push them, but packets sold only go up when people really want them.

screens.title: From their story to yours
screens.text: iD tested with a handful of stores before betting big, and you can do exactly the same with your own idea. Say you make homemade pickles and dream of opening a shop. Before you sign a lease, you take a stall at a Sunday market to test it.

screens.prompt: The stall costs ₹6,000 a month, and each jar leaves you ₹50. With 4 Sundays a month, how many jars a Sunday pay the stall?
screens.why: Well done. ₹6,000 ÷ ₹50 is 120 jars a month, and 120 ÷ 4 Sundays is 30. So 30 jars only pays the stall. Your yes number has to sit above it, or you're working for free.

wrong.b: I see what you did: ₹6,000 ÷ ₹50 = 120. But that's for the whole month, and there are 4 Sundays, so it's 30 jars each Sunday.
wrong.c: Not quite. ₹6,000 ÷ ₹50 = 120 jars a month, and split over 4 Sundays, that's 30 jars each Sunday.

screens.prompt: Each jar leaves ₹50 and the stall costs ₹6,000. The shop only makes sense if you clear ₹4,000 after rent. Which yes line?

options.label: Lots of people stop to taste
50 jars sold each Sunday by week 8

screens.why: Exactly. You need ₹6,000 for rent plus ₹4,000 left over, which is ₹10,000. At ₹50 a jar that's 200 jars a month, or 50 each Sunday. Now your number has a reason, it counts jars sold, and it has a date.

wrong.a: Tasting is free, so lots of people will do it. But your goal is ₹4,000 left after rent, and only paid jars get you there: 50 of them each Sunday.
wrong.c: You're right that the line must sit above 30, but how far above? Your ₹4,000 goal answers that: ₹10,000 ÷ ₹50 is 200 jars a month, or 50 each Sunday, by week 8.

screens.prompt: Your yes line was 50 jars a Sunday by week 8. You're selling 42. A friend says, 'Close enough, open the shop!' Your reply?

options.label: Not yet. Change one thing and test again

screens.why: Exactly. At 42 jars you make 42 × ₹50 × 4 = ₹8,400 a month, which leaves ₹2,400 after rent. That's decent, but you decided ₹4,000 was the bar for a shop. Change one thing, like a new flavour or a better spot, and test again, just as iD kept fixing its batter.

wrong.a: I see why 42 feels close. But it leaves ₹2,400 after rent, and you decided before the test that a shop needs ₹4,000. Don't let 'close' change the rule after you've seen the result.
wrong.b: That's moving the goalposts after the kick. This round missed, but that doesn't mean the idea is dead; it means you haven't earned the big bet yet. Change one thing and test again.

screens.prompt: A shop would cost ₹3 lakh to set up. Your stall test costs ₹6,000 a month for 2 months. What share is that?
screens.why: Exactly. 2 × ₹6,000 is ₹12,000, and ₹12,000 out of ₹3,00,000 is 4%, so you risk ₹4 to learn whether to risk ₹100. That's why a small test is a cheap option: you can stop, change course, or go big once it works.

wrong.a: 40% would be ₹1,20,000. The test is only ₹12,000, which is 4% of ₹3 lakh.
wrong.c: 0.4% would be just ₹1,200. The test is ₹12,000, which is 4% of ₹3 lakh.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six moves for your pickles. For each one, tell me: is it a small test, or a big bet?

items.text: Sell a new lime flavour at one Sunday stall
Sign a 3-year lease on a shop
Buy 500 kg of limes for the new flavour
Supply one office canteen for a month
Print 5,000 labels with a shop address

screens.why: Exactly. A test is cheap and easy to stop, while a bet locks your money in. Do the tests first, and let them earn you the bet.

screens.prompt: Put a good test in order.
steps: Write the yes number and the date
Run it, and count your numbers every Sunday
Check against the yes number on the date
screens.why: Well done. Because the yes number comes before the test, and you count every Sunday along the way, the numbers get to decide, not hope.

screens.text: iD missed its date but never moved its target. Write the ___ that means yes ___ the test starts.
screens.why: Exactly. iD missed its date but never moved its target; it changed the batter instead. That's what pre-set success criteria do for you: they keep the test honest when hope wants to move the line.

summary: Start with a small, cheap version of the idea, and work out what result would make the big bet worth it.
Write that yes number and the date before you start, and count something buyers control.
If you miss, don't move the line. Change the offer and test again.

cards.front: Your pre-set success criteria said 12. The test hit 8. What now?
cards.back: Pre-set success criteria are set before the test for a reason. Change the offer, not the line.

cards.front: Stall rent ₹9,000 a month. Each sale leaves ₹30. Open 30 days. Sales a day to break even?
